Zeenat, you're asking why I made such a fuss about that message on your phone? Let me tell you something from when your Pema Aunty was your age.
In my town near Darjeeling, a boy from the next school started waiting at my bus stop. One evening he stood very close and said, "If you tell anyone I'm here, you'll be sorry." I was fifteen and proud. My friends said, "Shout at him! Show him you're not scared."

Nilesh, you want to win tomorrow's debate by making the other side look silly? Sit down. Your Noor Nani lost a debate that way.
At sixteen I was the loudest girl in our school in Lucknow. The topic was whether girls should play cricket at school. I was for it. My opponent, a quiet boy, gave one good point: our school had no proper ground, only a small courtyard.

He stood, took a breath, and didn't shout. "Dilnaz is right about cost. That's a real problem. So my claim is: keep uniforms, but let the school run a second-hand uniform exchange. Our survey of forty students showed thirty felt less judged about clothes with uniforms."
The front rows leaned in to hear. A few people nodded.
Dilnaz caught his eye afterwards. "You took my point seriously. That was annoying," she said, grinning.
